requirements.requirement: Build an IPsec tunnel between node1 and node2 over the shared transit network
requirements.summary: IKEv2/PSK swanctl connection configured on both node1 (10.10.10.1) and node2 (10.10.10.2) over the transit link; swanctl -l on both sides shows ESTABLISHED IKE_SA and INSTALLED child SA with matching traffic selectors, and actual ESP packet counters incrementing (non-zero bytes/packets) confirming a live, functioning tunnel, not just configuration.

requirements.requirement: Carry the private networks (lan-a 192.168.10.0/24, lan-b 192.168.20.0/24) over the tunnel
requirements.summary: Child SA traffic selectors on both sides are configured and shown as local 192.168.10.0/24 / remote 192.168.20.0/24 (and vice versa), with routes on node3/node4 pointing the remote subnet via the local firewall's LAN IP, and traffic verified encapsulated (see req-4).

requirements.requirement: node3 and node4 reach each other by private address
requirements.summary: Bidirectional ping between node3 (192.168.10.2) and node4 (192.168.20.2) succeeded with 0% packet loss after the enc0/opt3 firewall workaround was applied.

requirements.requirement: Traffic between the private networks is encrypted in transit
requirements.summary: tcpdump captured on the transit interface (vtnet1) during an active ping between node3 and node4 shows only ESP packets between 10.10.10.1 and 10.10.10.2, with no plaintext ICMP visible; a parallel capture on the LAN-facing interface (vtnet2) confirms plaintext ICMP only appears on the private-network side, consistent with encryption occurring on the transit link.

requirements.requirement: Management access to firewalls is preserved after firewall rule changes
requirements.summary: Exec/SSH access to node1 and node2 remained functional after each configctl filter reload / rc.reload_all cycle, confirmed via successive 'echo alive' probes.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: node1 pre/post restart with recovery
requirements.summary: Baseline kern.boottime and ESTABLISHED/INSTALLED IPsec SA captured, native FreeBSD reboot issued, distinct post-reboot kern.boottime observed after reconnect, IPsec SA re-established and end-to-end ping (node3->192.168.20.2) confirmed working after node1's reboot. Cross-checked against fixed lifecycle boot-identity diff showing a changed boottime for node1 between before_prepare and after_executor.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: node2 pre/post restart with recovery
requirements.summary: Baseline kern.boottime and SA state captured, reboot issued, distinct post-reboot boottime observed, IPsec SA re-established after reboot, and end-to-end ping recovery confirmed (2 of 3 pings succeeded, consistent with brief SA renegotiation lag rather than a broken tunnel). Cross-checked against fixed lifecycle snapshot boottime diff.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: node3 pre/post restart with recovery
requirements.summary: Baseline boot_id and working ping captured, systemctl reboot issued, distinct post-reboot boot_id confirmed, route and end-to-end ping recovery verified. Matches the fixed lifecycle before_prepare/after_executor boot-identity diff.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: node4 pre/post restart with recovery
requirements.summary: Baseline boot_id and working ping captured, systemctl reboot issued, distinct post-reboot boot_id confirmed, route and end-to-end ping recovery verified. Matches the fixed lifecycle before_prepare/after_executor boot-identity diff.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct evidence: an IKEv2/PSK IPsec tunnel is established and actively passing traffic between node1 and node2 over the transit network, the private lan-a/lan-b subnets are carried as child-SA traffic selectors, node3 and node4 achieve 0%-loss bidirectional connectivity by private address, and a transit-interface tcpdump capture confirms only ESP (no plaintext) crosses the wire during that traffic. The independent provider-wide restart protocol was also executed correctly and completely for all four nodes, with pre-restart baseline, reboot, a distinct post-reboot boot identity, and confirmed recovery of IPsec SAs, routes, and end-to-end connectivity for each node, corroborated by the fixed lifecycle boot-identity snapshots. Hygiene is moderate: the work involved a legitimate, if somewhat exploratory, troubleshooting arc (discovering the enc0 policy-IPsec pf quirk) but left behind several config.xml backup files, one orphaned/non-functional firewall rule, and assorted diagnostic pcap/log files in /tmp on multiple nodes, plus one instance of the PSK secret appearing in plaintext command output during generation.
limitations: The node2 restart ping check (cmd-80cd716303ec4323) showed 2/3 packets received rather than a fully clean 3/3, though this is consistent with a brief SA renegotiation window rather than a broken recovery.

Backup config.xml files and diagnostic /tmp artifacts on node1/node2 were not independently confirmed removed or retained via the fixed lifecycle diff (which only reported on a small tmp-file sample), so their residual presence is inferred from the command timeline rather than directly observed in the final snapshot.

Whether the orphaned 'IPsec'-interface firewall rule causes any functional or security side effect (versus being purely inert) could not be independently verified beyond the executor's own pfctl inspection.
Operational hygiene cited unknown evidence IDs: cmd-c9d0629b4bbd4375

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing actions were purposeful and tied to configuring, debugging, or verifying the tunnel (a legitimate, if somewhat exploratory, troubleshooting arc around the OPNsense enc0/policy-IPsec pf filtering quirk). However several unnecessary residues remain uncleaned: (1) multiple generations of config.xml backup files (config.xml.bak1 through .bak6) were left on both node1 and node2 and never removed; (2) an orphaned, non-functional firewall pass rule bound to the friendly interface name 'IPsec' (originally 'ipsec') was added and then abandoned in favor of a working opt3/enc0-bound rule, leaving dead configuration behind; (3) numerous diagnostic tcpdump/pcap/log files were left in /tmp on all four nodes and some persisted across reboot per the after_executor lifecycle snapshot (e.g. /tmp/out.pcap, /tmp/td.log, /tmp/td3.log, /tmp/td4.log on node3; /tmp/icmp.pcap, /tmp/tcpdump.log, /tmp/tcpdump.pid on node4); (4) the PSK was generated with `openssl rand -base64 24` and the raw secret value appeared directly in captured command stdout, weakening the executor's claim that the secret was never exposed in plaintext output, even though later config dumps correctly redacted it. None of these are destructive, broad, or security-control-weakening, and the core LAN/transit firewall rules and IPsec configuration were retained and functional, so this is scored as a moderate rather than severe hygiene deduction.
